item.title: At least 9 new Dem members will carry Al Green's mantle and try to impeach President Trump
item.description: Rep. Al Green says at least nine incoming House Democratic caucus members will join his impeachment push, citing President Trump's crypto dealings and what they described as corruption.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: At least 9 incoming progressive members of the House Democratic caucus are expected to support efforts to impeach President Donald Trump, continuing a push led by outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, Fox News Digital has learned.

Green and representatives from the Removal Coalition and Courage for Democracy Project discussed the effort with Fox News Digital after a Capitol Hill news conference, months after the Texas Democrat introduced articles of impeachment against Trump in August.

Green is counting on support from Reps.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo.; Dan Koh, D-Mass.; Chris Rabb, D-Pa.; Angela Gonzales-Torres, D-Calif.; and several other incoming Democrats to continue his impeachment efforts after he leaves Congress.

DEMOCRAT AL GREEN TO FORCE HOUSE-WIDE VOTE ON IMPEACHING TRUMP

"Impeachment is the only means for our future. We cannot deal with a president who engages in corruption," Green told Fox News Digital. "The end is to have the president removed from office. I applaud the courageous members carrying these efforts into the next Congress."

Green pointed to Trump's cryptocurrency dealings as one example of what he characterized as corruption by the president.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE

Gonzales-Torres told Fox News Digital she intends to continue Green's efforts while representing the more than 100,000 Los Angeles voters she said elected her to Congress.

The coalition acknowledged uncertainty over whether its impeachment efforts would succeed, noting that even if the House approved articles against Trump, the Senate could again decline to convict him, as it did in Trump’s two previous impeachment trials.

TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS

However, organizers expressed confidence that growing grassroots pressure could persuade additional Democratic lawmakers to support impeachment.

"The more we articulate this effort and talk about why it is so crucial that we get rid of Trump, the more support we will have," Keira Havens, co-founder of the Courage for Democracy Project, told Fox News Digital.

Havens acknowledged that some Democrats who oppose Trump may still reject impeachment articles because they believe the allegations lack sufficient legal grounds or that conviction would fail in the Senate.

A constitutional expert affiliated with the Courage for Democracy Project also argued that Senate impeachment procedures could provide additional avenues for removing a president, citing Rule VIII. However, the Constitution gives the House the sole power of impeachment and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments.

PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

Jessica Denson, identified as the founder of the Removal Coalition, criticized Democratic lawmakers who have prioritized congressional hearings and potential prosecutions of Trump administration officials over impeaching the president himself.

Denson called those lawmakers "spineless," arguing that grassroots pressure could eventually push them to support the coalition's demands. The coalition told Fox News Digital that "hearings and prosecutions aren't enough," and enough public backlash will lead any remaining Democratic lawmaker to get behind impeachment efforts.

The effort comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, potentially giving impeachment supporters a greater opportunity to advance resolutions against Trump.

Under the Constitution, impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, while conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority of senators present.

During and after the news conference, the coalition, consisting of the two advocacy organizations and incoming and outgoing lawmakers, told Fox News Digital it also intends to pursue impeachment proceedings against War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The coalition argued that Hegseth should face impeachment alongside Trump, claiming that any wrongdoing uncovered involving the war secretary could also implicate the president.

However, a finding of wrongdoing by Hegseth would not automatically establish legal or constitutional liability for Trump.

Trump and Hegseth did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: New College Football Playoff poll proves the selection committee is just making it up as they go
item.description: Indiana Hoosiers dropped five spots during their bye week as Hunter Yurachek's explanations raise more questions about CFP committee consistency.
item.content:encoded:
They're at it again.

When the first poll from the College Football Playoff committee was released last week, it was immediately greeted with scorn, derision, frustration, and even anger from many fans and analysts who questioned how the rankings were determined.

The lapses in logic, clear mistakes, and often inexplicable justifications from committee chairman Hunter Yurachek during his post-release interview only served to make the poll appear worse. But given the widespread discontent and overwhelmingly negative feedback pouring towards the committee, there was some small sliver of hope that the week two poll might address some of the issues. Or at least, provide some acknowledgment that the committee had overcorrected for "strength of schedule" in favor of one specific conference.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF RANKINGS: GEORGIA RISE TO NO. 1, NOTRE DAME CRACKS TOP 5 AFTER BIG WIN OVER MIAMI

Well, hope everyone didn't get their hopes up too high, because week two's release on Tuesday night only served to reaffirm the same concerns and frustrations from week one. If not exacerbate them. This week's poll managed to take the clear bias towards one conference and make it even more obvious, while Yurachek's defense of an inexplicable ranking change only served to reaffirm that the committee is just making it all up as they go.

Let's start with the former No. 1 team in the country: the Miami Hurricanes.

Miami entered the week undefeated and the consensus top team in the rankings. They went on the road to play a highly regarded Notre Dame team, ranked No. 4 in the AP Poll and No. 11 in the CFB Playoff poll, without their best player, Malachi Toney. The Hurricanes had the ball 4th-and-6 with 3:36 to go at the Notre Dame 18-yard-line and seemed to complete a pass for a touchdown to tie the game. It looked like a catch in real time and on replay; the Miami receiver came down with a foot in bounds, then stepped out of bounds, before losing control of the ball. But the officials on the field called it incomplete and review upheld it. They lost 31-24, but that play served to underscore how close the outcome was.

Road loss to a highly-ranked team in a very close game, missing their best player. Surely, the Hurricanes dropped just a few spots, right? After all, that's the standard that poll voters have set for the SEC; lose a close game on the road to a highly-ranked team and you'll drop one spot. Maybe.

Instead, Miami fell six spots to No. 7. When the Georgia Bulldogs lost, at home, to a mediocre Auburn Tigers team, AP Poll voters dropped them four spots. That's why fans from other conferences get upset; there is very little consistency for how these "experts" evaluate losses, and the benefits always seem to point in one direction.

Speaking of absurd drops, one of Yurachek's most ridiculous post-poll comments was about the now-No. 9 Indiana Hoosiers. Indiana entered the week at No. 4 and didn't play, sitting out for their bye week ahead of a huge matchup against USC on Saturday. While not playing, they dropped from No. 4 to No. 9. Again, they did not play. And they dropped five spots.

Inexplicable, right? Well, Yurachek was asked about it and attempted to provide an explanation.

"Indiana was probably a victim of having a bye week at the wrong time with seven games between Top 25 teams," he said. "The committee is really impressed with what UCLA, Texas, and Notre Dame did as well as Alabama and LSU."

WE NEED TO ABOLISH THE CFP SELECTION COMMITTEE AFTER YET ANOTHER EMBARRASSMENT

"Every team that Indiana had played to date in the Big Ten all lost and that effected their strength of schedule rank and the committee's review of Indiana," he continued. "The quarterback play in general and the offensive play in general is kind of a discussion point of Indiana...They've won games because of their defense and not their offense."

Dear lord. This is nonsense. Who cares how Indiana wins? Why does that matter? When SEC teams dominated teams defensively, particularly Nick Saban's Alabama or the early Kirby Smart-era at Georgia, it was a testament to their toughness and quality and "defense wins championships" mindset. Now that Indiana is winning games with their defense, it's a negative? Alabama doesn't get punished for Mississippi State's collapse, but Indiana's opponents losing justifies this?

Indiana's non-conference schedule is frequently cited as unacceptably poor, yet per ESPN's own FPI computer metrics, the Hoosiers' best non-conference opponent, North Texas, would be an 8.5 point favorite over Georgia Tech, arguably UGA's "toughest" non-conference opponent. Georgia Tech is 2-7. Perception and brand names are often not reflective of reality.

Ironically, the committee was "impressed" with what UCLA did, which was beat Minnesota. The same Minnesota team that Indiana also beat the week before their bye. Yes, UCLA had a higher scoring margin, but since when has that mattered to the committee?

So Miami drops six spots after a close road loss to a top-11 team, Indiana drops five spots because they didn't play. Hilariously, the Kentucky Wildcats, who were exposed in a blowout loss to Tennessee, dropped just five spots as a result. There's plenty more to cover further down the rankings, but Kentucky's two losses are by 28 points and...28 points. They fell five spots. See why scoring margin matters, until it doesn't?

Further down the list are more absurdities.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

USC moved up two spots to No. 18 at 7-2. They're behind Iowa, also at 7-2, and multiple three-loss teams including South Carolina. Three losses. Missouri is also still ranked as a three loss team, with an extremely unimpressive resume.

The Tigers' non-conference schedule was awful; Arkansas Pine Bluff, Kansas, and Troy. They lost to Mississippi State, beat a bad and overrated Florida team, a bad Texas A&M team, got blown out by Ole Miss, beat a bad Arkansas team, and lost to Texas. That's a ranked team. Why? Because they play Kentucky this weekend, providing yet another opportunity for "ranked game" SEC posts.

In fact, they're ahead of Arizona, despite the Wildcats' two close losses coming on the road at BYU and Texas Tech. Speaking of Arizona, at 6-2 they had a one-possession win over 4-5 TCU at home and dropped a spot. South Carolina had a one-possession home win over 4-5 Texas A&M and moved up four spots.

LSU is still ranked, despite not having a single impressive win on their resume. Every game against a "quality" opponent, Ole Miss, Kentucky and Alabama, they've lost. But they did beat McNeese State 63-14, so they have that going for them.

Some have mentioned that Tennessee is five spots behind Alabama, despite the Volunteers' head-to-head win. But Yurachek hand-waves those concerns off because the two teams are not in the same made-up "pods" that the committee uses to compare teams. Head-to-head only matters until it doesn't.

The reality, as we've seen these past two weeks, is that the committee has no meaningful consistent standards. They make it up as they go. Strength of schedule is based mostly on perception and brand names. Head-to-head only matters sometimes. Injuries to key starting players matters, but only for certain positions and certain times.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

The committee is simply picking teams based on what they want the outcomes to look like, then creating post-hoc justifications for it afterward. Which is why there's no consistency week-to-week, Indiana drops five spots while not playing, and the explanations Yurachek provides are so easily dismissed.

What should be done? Well, that requires a longer explanation, but a start would be creating a clear set of standards that are consistently enforced. Transparency around the exact metrics the committee is using to create their "strength of schedule" claims, not just "we think this win looks better now" week-to-week changes. Will we get it? Absolutely not. Will these rankings continue being a farce? Without question.

item.title: Jeffries promises ‘remedial assistance’ to anyone impacted by Trump immigration enforcement
item.description: Hakeem Jeffries pledged to drive down cost of living on housing, healthcare, and groceries, but he also vowed remedial assistance for DACA recipients.
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., pledged "remedial assistance" to anyone he claimed had been treated "unfairly" by the Trump administration's immigration policies during an interview on Tuesday.

After mentioning his commitment to affordability for Americans, Jeffries — who is hoping to be Speaker of the House in the new Congress next year — was asked on PBS about whether he would support DACA recipients being brought back to the U.S. amid the Trump administration's crackdown.

"Certainly anyone, whether they are a citizen, whether they were here lawfully, whether there are DACA recipients [who have] been treated unfairly and unjustly by the administration, we need to provide remedial assistance to them and undo the damage that's been done to the country, to law-abiding immigrant families, and to the American people over this last 20 months or so," he said.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE

His interviewer noted President Donald Trump said he hoped to work with Democrats after they swept into the majorities in both chambers last week.

Jeffries touted a recent bipartisan housing affordability bill and said Democrats were committed to driving down the cost of living.

"That's housing, that's healthcare, that's groceries, that's gas, that's caregiving, and making this country affordable again for everyone," he said.

JEFFRIES VOWS DEMOCRATS WON’T ‘GIVE A DIME’ TO TRUMP’S DEPORTATION EFFORTS

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital, "Democrats show time and time again with their extremist, anti-American policies that they care more about illegal aliens than U.S. citizens."

No one wants to see violent deportations, but 80% of voters opposed the Biden immigration fiasco and nearly that many oppose amnesty," he wrote. item.title: Kirk Cousins reveals touching decision his sons made after trade to Vikings: 'Let's go!'
item.description: Kirk Cousins revealed his Minnesota home sold quickly after joining Atlanta, and now his sons chose to leave Las Vegas to watch him play for the Vikings.
item.content:encoded:
Kirk Cousins is back with the Minnesota Vikings, and while he needs to get caught up to speed with Kevin O’Connell’s offensive scheme once more, he also needs to figure out where his family is going to be staying.

Cousins revealed that his Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota home was sold "pretty quickly" when he signed with the Atlanta Falcons, which means starting anew with this return to the Vikings following a trade deadline deal the Las Vegas Raiders made.

But while Cousins’ wife, Julie, is working on the home situation, the veteran quarterback was thrilled to also reveal his two sons, Cooper and Turner, wanted to head north and leave Sin City to watch their dad hopefully turn things around in Minnesota.

It was their call.

"I was hoping they were going to come with me, but I said, ‘What are you thinking, Julie?’ I know it was her call," Cousins said after a reporter asked about his living situation. "She said, ‘I don’t think I can pull the boys out of school, and baseball, and their friends.’ She picked them up from school and said, ‘Here’s the situation: dad got traded to the Minnesota Vikings. What would you guys want to do?’

"They looked at her and said, ‘Let’s go!’ So, they’re across the street [in a hotel] and they’re ready and excited for the next several weeks."

One reporter joked and asked if the boys, now nine and seven years old, would be helping shovel with the winter snows coming soon in Minnesota.

"Well, we gotta get a driveway first," Cousins said, laughing. "I don’t have a driveway, so one day at a time. But Julie’s handling that."

Cousins added earlier that his neighbor had a prospective buyer once he signed his three-year deal with the Falcons in 2024, which led to a very quick sale that didn’t result in a listing. But Cousins couldn’t anticipate he’d ever be back in Minnesota.

However, the Vikings haven’t had quarterback bliss since Cousins’ departure. Sam Darnold had a fantastic 14-3 season in 2024, but he joined the Seattle Seahawks the following season, ultimately leading them to a Super Bowl.

O’Connell and the Vikings were hoping J.J. McCarthy, their 2024 first-round pick who couldn’t go his rookie year due to a meniscus injury, would be the quarterback of the future starting in 2025 when Darnold walked. But his up-and-down play, and reported character issues, led to the signing of Kyler Murray this past offseason.

Since then, Murray hasn’t been able to stay healthy, nor consistent, on the field, while McCarthy was made third string and eventually traded to the New York Giants following the season-ending injury for their own franchise quarterback, Jaxson Dart.

McCarthy has done well since he was named the Giants’ starter, going 2-0 in his starts, while the Vikings just tested Carson Wentz after Murray was too injured to play "Monday Night Football" against the Buffalo Bills. Wentz’s performance was so bad, it became clear quickly on deadline day Tuesday that Minnesota was looking desperately for a quarterback to hopefully provide competent quarterback play to pair with a Super Bowl-caliber defense.

Cousins was the man, and it seemed easy for the Vikings to want him considering the previous connection and work in O’Connell’s scheme. With Cousins’ understanding of the scheme, as well as chemistry with receivers like Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, we could see the Vikings’ offense finally sustain drives, and hopefully for their own sake, produce points on the scoreboard.

Cousins is excited for the opportunity to work with the Vikings again, especially considering things were not going well in Las Vegas despite a 3-0 start. The Raiders are now 4-5, and the decision was made to hand the ball over to Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick of the 2026 NFL Draft who had been backing up and learning from Cousins.

It will be a busy week for the 38-year-old signal caller, but everyone in Minnesota, including his entire family which is ready to plant its roots soon in a new home, will be behind him in this next chapter.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Jewish physician wins religious exemption from union membership and fees over Israel stances
item.description: Dr. Jacob Agronin secured a full religious accommodation from SEIU union dues after citing the union's anti-Israel stances and calls to boycott the Jewish state.
item.content:encoded:
A Jewish doctor has been granted an exemption from union membership and fees after he challenged a requirement to financially support a union that he said violated his religious beliefs.

Dr. Jacob Agronin, a physician at Temple University Hospital in Philadelphia, secured the accommodation after America First Legal (AFL) brought the matter to the Committee of Interns and Residents (CIR), Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1957, demanding that the union exempt the doctor from membership and fees.

AFL cited the union's stances on Israel, including endorsing the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and accusing the Jewish state of apartheid and genocide.

CIR’s collective bargaining agreement with Temple University Hospital required employees covered by the agreement to join the union or pay agency fees, according to AFL.

NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK

"[Agronin] wasn't objecting to the union's right to political speech," Megan Redshaw, counsel for AFL, told Fox News Digital. "The union can have whatever views it wants to have. However, when the union imposes its views in the workplace and that affects the people that work at that organization, that institution, or that hospital, this becomes a Title VII issue."

Redshaw said Agronin believed financially supporting the union in any capacity would violate his religious beliefs, even if payments supporting political activities were excluded.

The union confirmed in an Oct. 9 letter that it had granted the accommodation and that Agronin had neither signed a membership card nor paid dues.

"No fees will be taken out of his paycheck, his employer will honor that and he does not have to be a member of the union at all," Redshaw told Fox News Digital. She also explained that Agronin’s request cited "Jewish law and Jewish beliefs" to explain why supporting the union conflicted with his faith.

CIR says it represents "over 40,000 resident physicians and fellows who are dedicated to improving residency training and education, advancing patient care and expanding healthcare access for our communities."

Redshaw accused CIR of using members’ dues to advance political and ideological causes that "nobody knows they're signing up for when they agree to join this union," while the union promotes its ability to improve pay and working conditions.

POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATIONS PUT PUBLIC SCHOOLS UNDER THE MICROSCOPE

In May 2024, CIR adopted two resolutions regarding Israel: "Housestaff for Human Rights" and "Housestaff Against Apartheid."

The union stated that the first resolution "set standards to ensure CIR will not endorse candidates who accept donations from the Israel lobby or who otherwise support genocide and apartheid" and the second resolution called for a permanent ceasefire and the end of military aid to Israel. Additionally, according to the union, the "Housestaff Against Apartheid" resolution also "uplifted" the BDS movement.

On Nov. 7, 2023, one month after Hamas launched its Oct. 7 attacks on Israel, CIR released a statement saying it was "appalled and shocked by the recent violence in Israel and Palestine." The union said it mourned the lives lost in the Oct. 7 attacks and those lost in the subsequent violence.

In its statement, CIR called on the Biden administration and Congress to help restore access to food, water, electricity, housing and healthcare in Gaza and ensure the release of the hostages and "Palestinians detained in Israel without due process." It also urged the administration and Congress to "call for an immediate ceasefire."

In May 2026, as part of his written testimony to the House Education and Workforce Committee's Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions for a hearing titled "Bad Medicine: Politics, Unions, and Antisemitism in Health Care," Agronin referenced the November 2023 statement.

Agronin acknowledged the parts of the statement that "mourned Israeli and Palestinian casualties, called for hostage release and condemned antisemitism and Islamophobia," while also objecting to other parts of the statement. The physician noted that Hamas was not named in the statement, said the "Palestinian casualty figures are uncritically cited" and called the antisemitism condemnation "subordinated."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The physician also objected to the statement's presentation of Israeli and Palestinian casualties "in morally equivalent terms," adding that doing so "implicitly treats the perpetrators and victims of October 7th as equivalent parties."

Redshaw said physicians with similar religious objections may be able to secure full exemptions from union membership and fees.

"Most people believe that in requesting religious accommodation, you're just going to get an accommodation from the fees that are taken out for these political or ideological causes, or they think that that fee that's taken out has to go to a charity, usually of CIR's choosing," she told Fox News Digital. 

"Which is nefarious in and of itself, because the union can just choose a charity that perpetuates its causes that it believes in and transfer your money there," Redshaw added. 

"But the reality of this situation is that, depending on the state that you're in, you can request a full religious accommodation. You can object to being a member of the union as a whole." 

CIR and Temple University Hospital did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
